utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could be brought in. While that is happening, could I just mention to guide and assist counsel that on this Friday it will be necessary for the Chamber to adjourn at about 12.30 rather than 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And on Monday, the 6th of June, it will be necessary to adjourn at about 5.45. There will be yet another special meeting of Judges to consider proposals to change court procedures, so we will have to shorten the hearings on those two days for that purpose. Good afternoon, Mr. Sopi. If I could remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. The court officer will switch on your microphones and we'll be ready to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are we tuned into the correct channel for the witness? Could you just check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I say that I did remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Sopi, I'm going to ask you a few questions now, not too many. The same as yesterday, we need to speak a little bit slowly to allow for the interpretation. And if you have any problems understanding my questions or hearing me through the headphones, let us know right away.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You went over your background in the questioning by Mr. Mansfield in some detail and I just want to go over that again a little bit. You were born in Lapusnik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I gather that other than your military service and brief periods working abroad, you've lived most of your life in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in the same house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And today, you still have an extended family in Lapusnik, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also talked about how life in Lapusnik was very hard under the Serb oppression before the war?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not just in Lapusnik but in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you came to the conclusion, the people, that the only way out of this oppression was to fight?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the only ones to fight at that time were the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no other possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. And speaking now about Lapusnik. The whole population of Lapusnik supported the KLA from May 1998 onwards, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Every KLA member was like a family member to people in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it goes without saying that the entire Sopi family always supported the KLA in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the Sopi family, but Gashi, Thaqi, Krasniqi families. All families that were in Lapusnik supported the KLA as if they were their own family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. Letting KLA members stay in your homes?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all houses starting from the school at Lapusnik and to the school in Kishna Reka. All this was a KLA military barracks. Due to difficult circumstances and continuous shelling, it was necessary to change the places where they rested. It wasn't safe to stay just in one house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you're proud of your service in the KLA, aren't you, your help to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm proud.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You yourself were a member of the Pellumbi unit?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Celiku unit in the beginning but in the end of June I went to Pellumbi unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And your son was a member of Celiku 3?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the KLA, yes, but he was in Celiku 3 unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you just tell me if he had a pseudonym in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And because of their defence of Lapusnik, you've described the KLA members who came from outside of Lapusnik as holy and as sacred. Correct? You did that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This is what I said and it goes not only for me but for the entire population of Lapusnik, because as I mentioned yesterday the Serbs came to our thresholds and they, the KLA, were there to rescue the population and that's why they were sacred. The population was scared, seeing what had happened in Likoshan, Qirez, and Prekaz.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could you tell me the name of your son who was in Celiku 3?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Bekim Sopi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And yesterday you described the three accused in this case as friends; that's how you view them, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Comrades in arms. I didn't know Fatmir and Isak Musliu before 9th of May. As for Haradin, I knew him from my childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The people in Lapusnik follow this trial pretty closely in the media, don't they?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's in the papers almost every day as well as being on television.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we didn't get this yesterday I don't think in your background, but you're currently in the TMK. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what your position is.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am the commander of the transport battalion and my rank is a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you now just a couple of questions about the Pellumbi unit, make sure I'm clear. You joined the Pellumbi Unit, the north side of the Pristina-Peja road, in June?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the end of June. I don't remember the date, but it was in the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And until 26th of July, then you were with that Pellumbi unit working shifts at your assigned position?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when your shift was done, whether it was day or night, you would walk back to your house on the other side of the road to sleep?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because my house was nearby and that's why I always went to sleep in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the KLA fought in Lapusnik until 26th July, when all of the soldiers and the population were forced to quickly flee into the hills?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the people unfortunately had to leave virtually everything behind. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything they had they left behind. Some old men who were not -- who were unable to leave remained in their houses, and the Serb forces found them in their houses. There's a person called Bajram Gashi who was killed in his house and whose body was burned. He was of the age 85 or 86.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the soldiers also had to leave very quickly and bring almost nothing with them?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There wasn't any possibility to take anything with them. I mentioned yesterday as well that on that day the Lapusnik gorge was attacked by 140 cannons -- correction, tanks. They used cannons, hand-held rocket launchers. I don't know the name of the equipment because I'm not a military person; therefore, for them it wasn't possible for them to take anything with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about a man named Ruzhdi Karpuzi who came to Lapusnik around the 9th of May. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Ruzhdi Karpuzi very well. I know that he came to Lapusnik but I don't remember the date when he came. I don't know the date, but I know Ruzhdi. He had problems with his leg and to my knowledge and what I was told by my friend, Ruzhdi injured the same leg on the 26th of July and is an invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. When he came to Lapusnik he was suffering because of an injury he'd had before the war and he had a bad limp, didn't he, to he was allowed to do some lighter duty in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what he did was keep records in the oda of Gzim Gashi's compound, the same compound where you would eat your meals in June and July?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you what he did, but as the number of the KLA soldiers grew bigger in Lapusnik, he began to take notes, to keep records of soldiers who were coming to Lapusnik in order to prepare a report that was necessary for guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And my point is: Part of the reason he didn't that, isn't it, is because you describe the work going on, ditches being dug. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that he stayed there during calm days; however, when there was fighting going on I always saw him at positions as well, fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was no need for him to keep records that much. There were only 24, 25 soldiers at that time. And as I said, this number grew bigger later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Haradin Bala, you've personally known him since childhood?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And besides that, your family has close family ties with his family. You talked about -- I'm not sure if I remember correctly, your -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You described yesterday seeing him in Lapusnik. My question is: Did he take part in an intense -- in fighting between the 17th and 19th of May or was he too sick?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't remember whether he took part in an intense 17-hour fire-fight during those days?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was such an intense fighting on the 29th of May, not on the 17th to 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know that's what you said. I'm asking you about the 17th to 19th.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying 17th or 19th of May. What I said was that I saw him on the 29th [Realtime transcript read in error: "19th"] of May when Kumanova called Haradin Bala and asked him, Why are you here and you should come with me to Luznica. This is what I said; I did not mention 17th or 19th because I don't remember the dates seven years after the events. One can remember some more important dates as the 9th of May or 26th of July. However, I cannot remember other dates. The 29th of May for me is a date easily remembered because the fighting went on for 17 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And you're right, Mr. Sopi, you said "29th" yesterday. I was asking you about the 17th and 19th as well. What kind of car did Haradin Bala have? You said you saw him with a car.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You have no idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't -- I apologise for interrupting. However, I believe there's a minor mistake on line 12 of page 8. It should be the 29th of May, not the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said that Haradin Bala moved his family to Bajice. How did he move them there?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Baince, not Bajice. He moved his family to Baince. This is a village situated between Nekovce and Sedlare, or Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not very good with the pronunciations. But how did he move them there was the question.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't with him. I heard that Haradin moved his family. And when you're asking me about his car, I mentioned yesterday that I saw him in August 1998 in Novoselle and he had a Lada vehicle. Whether this Lada was his or belonged to his friends, this I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You said yesterday that Fatmir Limaj rarely came to Lapusnik and when he came he came to fight. Do you remember saying that? The question is just: Do you remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you met with the Defence before coming here to testify. Correct? And there's nothing wrong with that. I just want to know whether you met with the Defence before you testified.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you tried to give them some sense of what you were going to testify to. Correct? You told them your story as completely and accurately as you could.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. What I remember and know, I have the honour to say that before this Honoured Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, they gave us a summary of what you are expected to testify to and I just want to read you part of it. "The witness will testify that he has seen the accused Fatmir Limaj on 9 May in Lapusnik. After the fighting, the accused Fatmir Limaj left to return in the company of Kumanova twice when the fighting continued." Now, that's an entirely correct statement, isn't it, of when you saw Fatmir Limaj in Lapusnik between May and July 1998?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had seen him seven or eight times. On 9th of May I talked with Fatmir Limaj after the Serb forces withdrew. But I didn't know him as Fatmir. However, I heard soldiers who were there calling him Daja. I didn't see him with Kumanova on the 9th of May. I don't remember seeing Kumanova. There were many soldiers there, but I don't remember seeing him. I saw Kumanova on the 29th of May at Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, what you told the Defence is that you saw Fatmir Limaj three times. Right? On the 9th of May and then on two more occasions.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that maybe I have said that. Maybe the translation was not correct, but what I said was that I saw him more than three times, seven or eight times. As I explained yesterday, on Saturdays and Sundays, when international organisations operating in Kosova at that time were on holidays, the Serb forces took advantage of this and attacked us on the weekends. This is what I said. I don't remember saying that I've seen him three times. I remember saying that I've seen him seven or eight times and I always saw him at positions and in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the main fighting, as you've said, was on the 9th of May, 29th of May, and 26th of July. That's three times, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you hear about an oath ceremony in June?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember the date but I know very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was in Bali Vojvoda's compound?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you saw Fatmir Limaj there giving a speech then?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him. It wasn't a speech but he read the text of the oath. This lasted for 15 or 20 minutes and then we dispersed. Those who were on duty went back to their duties, to their positions; and those who were not on duty, they went back to the houses where they were resting. Fatmir went to his own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That place, Bali Vojvoda 's compound where the oath ceremony took place is across the road from Gzim Gashi's compound, correct? Not directly across but across the street.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And -- I forgot to ask you, did you have a pseudonym May, June, July?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you know there's another compound directly across the street from Gzim Gashi's compound. Right?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Directly across from the kitchen where you ate every day?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In June and July, you saw soldiers, KLA soldiers, going in and out of that compound, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is the compound next to Bali Vojvoda's?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You know that that compound was used as a prison by the KLA before the 26th of July when Lapusnik fell?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this only after the arrest of my friends, about this group of houses. When I saw KFOR forces, which surrounded the entire neighbourhood, I asked in the neighbourhood what was going on, and that's where I found out that that house was supposed to have served as a prison. Secondly, I would like to tell this Court that I have filmed my house, which served as a KLA warehouse. I have filmed Ferat Sopi's house. I have filmed the sheltering place in my house and the KLA Gulinov that was seized. The Serb forces filmed all this and I wonder why they didn't film the house of my neighbour and those alleged traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When exactly was your house a warehouse, used as a warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my house that I marked yesterday with number 1. I have brought pictures with me; the Defence lawyers have them. I brought pictures of my house, how it was burned after the war. You can see clearly the sheltering place --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop. My question is: When was your house used as a KLA warehouse? When?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, from 9th of May until the 26th, everything, food supplies, everything remained behind. My house was burned five or six days later. Other houses in Lapusnik were not burned on the 25th or 26th of July. Only the outpatient clinic. The houses of Ferat Sopi and Afrim Sopi. The other houses were not burned. The other houses were burned after 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've answered my question about when. You knew yourself during the summer of 1998 when you were eating at Gzim Gashi's kitchen that there was a prison across the road. Did you ever go into that compound?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've answered the question. You know that Haradin Bala was a guard at that prison?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You saw him coming to pick up food at Gzim Gashi's compound. Did you think he was picking it up for soldiers or for prisoners? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who? Who are you referring to? Haradin?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Haradin Bala picking up food at Gzim Gashi's compound, did he tell you it was for soldiers or prisoners or what? At Gzim Gashi's kitchen.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct because Haradin Bala came and had his meals together with other comrades and then went to his duty for the time he was in Lapusnik. I didn't see Haradin Bala bringing food to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So your testimony is you ate with him in the kitchen in Gzim Gashi's compound but you never saw him bringing food for other people? Right?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw him bringing food for other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not even going to talk about the Serb prisoners, but you know there were Albanian men kept in that prison in atrocious conditions?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. As I said earlier, I heard about this only after the arrest of my friends. And you cannot find a person at Lapusnik who knows or who will tell you that there was a prison at Lapusnik because it was difficult on the first front line, and we couldn't endure them there ourselves, and -- let alone take prisoners. I never saw or heard for such a prison until these men were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll agree with you that there's nobody in Lapusnik who will tell us that there was a prison there. And I'll put it to you that you know men were there, you know they were chained to the walls, you know they were beaten, you know they were murdered. You didn't like it, perhaps, but you couldn't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I didn't come here to lie. I came here and took the oath before this Trial Chamber to tell the truth and nothing but the truth, to tell you what I know. If you allow me, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you've answered, and I think you just can't tell the truth about crimes committed in Lapusnik by people you consider sacred and holy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, it's not appropriate for you to put your view of the witness to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can't tell the truth here about crimes committed by people you consider sacred and holy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter that's arisen this afternoon. He indicated that he'd taken photographs, and I think you have them in batch 1. May I just check. You should have photocopies of it -- sorry, it may be the wrong batch number -- sorry, batch 2, batch 2. And if I may just show this bundle of photographs to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How does this arise, Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, he's asked -- he's been asked about photographs that he took. We have them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, he hasn't been asked. He volunteered that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, we have them. I'm not concerned -- I didn't -- haven't introduced them so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the point I'm getting at. They came up not in response to a question and they were not pursued in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I'm perfectly happy not to pursue it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you want to re-open you can approach it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No, no, I don't. Then I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Sopi, thank you very much. That concludes the questions that are to be put to you. So you are now free to leave and return to your home and other affairs. The court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, if I may. The next witness hopefully again is outside the door. Dr. Bajram Rexhepi, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm getting worried about it what you keep outside the door, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: He should be there. It depends on what door you mean. He should be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't want to mean you overlooked, Mr. Guy-Smith, but I take it from what you were appearing that you had no thought of re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did not. I just wanted to make sure I was communicating with the Chamber because at an early point my head was in some papers and you had to call my name. So I want to make sure we're working with each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We tend to get your signals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please take the card that's offered to you and read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Bajram Rexhepi. I represent Fatmir Limaj, who sits behind me, as you know. May I just remind you that we need to speak slowly for the interpreters, and so a pause is sometimes required to allow the interpreter to finish what they have to say. I'd kindly ask if you'd do the same. Now, the first question I put in leading form because I think there's no issue: By profession you are in fact a medical doctor. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes. I am a medical doctor, general surgery department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And are you currently a member of parliament in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a member of Kosova parliament of the second political group, according to the votes, and that is the Kosova Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Between March of 2002 and December 2004, were you prime minister of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes. To be more precise, from 4th of March, 2002, until 2nd of December, 2004. A little bit less than four years -- than three years, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: During that time, did you know Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes. I came to know Mr. Fatmir Limaj sometime in August 1999 and mostly in September 1999 when we travelled to the United States for a conference. And later on, during party activities and activities at the parliament. And he was a close collaborator of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I ask you about the visit to the United States in September 1999. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: The purpose of this visit was for some current leaders of Kosova of the majority Albanian community and the Serbian community and other minorities to go to a joint conference in order to establish human relations between us and create conditions for joint future. To my knowledge, at that time the Serbian community was not ready to participate and they participated during the second conference in early house [as interpreted] when we actually had representatives of the Serbian ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And can I ask you who you met at this conference, yourself and Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: We went together at this conference with Fatmir Limaj and with others. The conference was organised by the peace institution of the United States. We spent there several days. We came forward with our proposals regarding the direction that Kosova should take in the future and regarding the best ways of democratisation for Kosova. I think that was a very important conference which resulted in fruitful conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Was the conference attended by any representatives of the United States government or the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: There were representatives of the American State Department, and as I mentioned earlier representatives of the peace institute of the United States and representatives of different associations. There were also representatives, to my knowledge, of the UNMIK mission in Kosova, but I don't remember their names. At that time, as far as I remember, it was Jan Kickert and several other councillors of Mr. Kushner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to take you back to Kosovo from matters international and ask you generally what Fatmir Limaj's role was in the post-war years.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: As I said earlier, at the beginning of August or beginning of September, I have known Fatmir Limaj. We were members of the same political party. Initially it was called the Party of Democratic Prosperity and later the name changed into the Democratic Party of Kosova. At that time I was appointed chairman of the Mitrovice municipality. And now and again we had contacts on a central level. Fatmir Limaj was a young leader with a vision. He was very open, very transparent, very close to us. And why not? He was dear to most of the citizens of Kosova, not only to the members of the political party he belonged, but in general. He was well-beloved and willing to help in every respect we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, could you please elaborate on what you understood his vision Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: His vision was that after bloody war in Kosova, a war where all of us participated, myself too as a surgeon [realtime transcript read in error: "searcher"] on account of our common ideal we should create a calm environment where all the citizens of Kosova would be able to lead a better life to democratise the life in Kosova and make it work in line with the other states of Europe. As to a longer-term vision, in addition to the independence of Kosova, which was our common goal, we would gradually on the basis of the implementation of several criteria over a longer-term period we become part of the European Union. These were our objectives. And we were all devoted to nondiscrimination of other communities, as we were in the past, but to contribute for a free life for all the citizens of Kosova and to provide to them a better perspective. This is more or less in general about his vision because I could elaborate it more if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just before we move on there's a slight error. In line 25, page 19, "myself too as a searcher" I think it should read "surgeon." So if that could be --

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes, surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, the question I want to ask you on the back of your answer is how Fatmir Limaj set about the task of realising the vision, putting it into effect.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: As far as I know, initially he was a member of a provisional council which was formed by the special envoy of the general secretary [as interpreted], where leaders of various parties held meetings. But our objective to realise this vision was through party activities; through elections, which followed later; through respect for law; through respect for internationals and in real terms with the UN mission in Kosova; and through other international representatives where everyone -- every citizen of Kosova be free to express his views, his religion, his culture views, to enjoy all rights and for the coming generations not to be traumatised by the war in the Balkans, as the case had been until then. Mr. Fatmir Limaj was held in high esteem by the main leaders of the Kosova Democratic Party, and he was secretary for international relations. After the first parliamentary elections, he was the leader of the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party of Kosova, and he was very cooperative and very tolerant and friendly with all his comrades, not only with the political parties of the Albanian majority but of the other communities, including the Serb community. If you allow me, Your Honours, I'd like to say that this man had the courage and the bravery since the very first days after the war to extend his hand to the representatives of the Serb community, unlike some other politicians who were rather hesitant at that time to do the same. So I have always admired him for his courage and his readiness to do that after all what happened in Kosova, to find the strength and work toward reconciliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: In the context of that answer, is it right - again, I think there's no issue about this - that in 2003 following the arrest of Fatmir Limaj, representatives of all the ethnic minority groups signed a letter to this Tribunal indicating their support for Fatmir Limaj in the work that he's done in relation to those matters you've just mentioned, namely the work towards a multi-cultural society?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fatmir Limaj is missing to the political life in Kosova and to parliament. The minority communities have lost a powerful supporter in the fight for their rights in Kosova in general, in parliament in particular. They have -- all the communities, non-Serb communities, have, including the Turks, the Bosnians, the Egyptians, the Romas, Ashkalis, have signed a letter of support for Fatmir Limaj. And if you allow me, I'd like to give a detail that in the few contacts we had with the Serb communities, they too supported him privately. But it was because of the Serbian policy that they couldn't openly voice their support for such a frank man, as they themselves admitted; something which we understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to -- well, first I give you an opportunity. Is there anything else you want to say about Fatmir Limaj in the post-war period? Because I want to now turn to the day of his arrest.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes. I may say that we have been connected by a common activity, working in the same political entity in the Democratic Party of Kosova. For a short time, I too was a member of parliament; then I was elected in prime minister. Then I want to say with full sincerity without any demagoguery that he was one of the best collaborators, a man willing to help whenever he was called for, a man who loves life, a man who was willing to work for the future of Kosova, a just man, a man who might have maintained different positions but a man who is willing to accept alternatives, to accept arguments. Personally I have to say that he was a very beloved man for me. Like him, there are other members in the Democratic Party where I am -- at here. I could unhesitatingly declare that he is a man who has deserved my respect, whom I have always appreciated. He is -- and his readiness. He has always been a humane person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just before I move to the arrest, looking at Kosovo at the moment, at the present, in what ways do you think he could make a constructive contribution right now, were he to be able to?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: I don't know how well-informed you are of the current developments in Kosova. After the second parliamentary election, when in our parliament we have the ruling party and the opposition, this is the first time for us to have that. We really miss Mr. Limaj's presence because often we have arguments in our parliament even when we shouldn't do that. And when we had Fatmir Limaj, he was a man who could -- who knew how to talk, even with the political adversaries, and be close to the representatives of the other communities. So such a man, as I said, we miss and we can feel the outcomes of not having the presence of such man when we are criticised sometimes, for the fierce opposition existing between the ruling party and the minority party. If Mr. Limaj would be in parliament, such a situation wouldn't be so tense; the frictions would be less severe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a particular day and the events leading up to that particular day in 2003 when Fatmir Limaj was arrested. The day itself was the 18th of February in that year. Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that day. It was a day of real despair for myself when I heard that Mr. Fatmir Limaj was accused by the Tribunal in The Hague. I personally was in my office as prime minister. I was busy with my meetings and it was about 4.00 in the afternoon that I received a call by Mr. Limaj informing me that he had heard from Reuters news agency, from a reporter called Shaban Buza that he was charged by the ICTY. At that time Mr. Limaj was on vacation in Slovenia, if I'm not wrong, near Kranjska Gora. I too was invited to go with him, but because of my numerous obligations I was unable to go with him. So we asked for a meeting with the representative of the General Secretary, Mr. Steiner, and with KFOR, General Fabio Mini to inform them that once Mr. Limaj was informed of the indictment he's willing to surrender voluntarily to the ICTY. But he wanted to come to Kosova first to greet his family and then and according to the procedures he might voluntarily surrender to the ICTY. As a prime minister of Kosova, but as a friend of Fatmir Limaj as well, I contacted Mr. Steiner even though he was very busy and then after half an hour we met -- actually met. Together with me was a former minister of public information, Mr. Jakup Krasniqi, and Ramadan Avdiu, my first political advisor. We informed him of our phone conversation with Mr. Limaj. Mr. Steiner expressed his readiness to -- to provide a special plane. If you allow me to explain this. He has a plane at his disposal, a UN plane, that he go to Slovenia on the 19th of February in the morning, fetch Mr. Fatmir Limaj, and bring him to Kosova and then to accompany him while he was meeting with his family and then to surrender him. During the conversation with Mr. Steiner, he said he was fully willing to do that because he too respected Mr. Limaj and he thought that if Fatmir Limaj were allowed to come as a normal passenger, maybe the Slovenian authorities would have arrested him. So while we discussed the technical aspects of Mr. Limaj's return to Kosova, it was about 6.00 I think in the evening when we were informed that the Slovenian police or the security service had gone to the place where Fatmir Limaj was resting and told him why they were there and he voluntarily surrendered. So we had to give up our procedures since he had already surrendered to the Slovenian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, just one or two questions arising from that. I think it follows that you knew that Fatmir Limaj was going on a holiday before he went. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes. Fatmir Limaj was on holiday together with Mr. Hashim Thaqi, the PDK chairman. And as I said earlier, before going on this holiday they invited me, too, to join them for four or five or maximum a week. But because of my engagements, I was unable to go with them. So they went together skiing and we had no idea that he would be one of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did you know when he was going on the holiday?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I think it was three or four days before the 18th, when they were on this vacation in Kranjska Gora. Because of our busy schedule, we didn't have much contact as to how they were doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to be precise. Did you know exactly where they were going before they went?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: If I understand, you're right, Your Honour. They set out to leave for Slovenia to go skiing. This is my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did you know the place in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: I was there before myself. And from sports activities going on there, Kranjska Gora is the place, if they were exactly there. I know more or less where that place is. But I didn't go on a vacation myself there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You mentioned a little earlier that you requested a meeting with General Fabio Mini who was the general in charge of KFOR. So far as you know, did he also know that Fatmir Limaj had left the country and gone on holiday?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to speculate and answer instead of Fabio Mini, but I'll refer to the previous arrest of three members of the KLA a day earlier. I think that Mr. Fabio Mini must have had information even though maybe it might be interpreted as speculation. Because together with Mr. Mini we didn't discuss this. I wanted to ask this general to enable the return of Fatmir Limaj, but Mr. Steiner, the special envoy, asked me to meet only with him because he said he was responsible for the peacekeeping mission in Kosova and if the need be, he would call the general, Fabio Mini. So I would suppose that he knew. But maybe. As I said, this is my only supposition. It may not be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, when the -- a phone call came through from Fatmir Limaj, did he tell you where he was at that time? Or if you can't remember, say so.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: I don't remember the details, but they told me they were in a hotel at a skiing place. And if I am not mistaken, since I was very busy with my engagements, it was in the vicinity of Kranjska Gora, but it may be as well elsewhere. I can't insist, because a long time has passed since then and maybe I have forgotten some details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The meeting you had with Mr. Steiner, the representative of the SRSG, where was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: This meeting was in the office of the SRSG, whom in the future I'll refer to as SRSG. Present were myself, former minister Jakup Krasniqi, and former advisor Avdiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, during that meeting, did you tell the SRSG where Fatmir Limaj was?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes. I told him that Mr. Fatmir Limaj is in Slovenia skiing on a vacation. But as to the exact location, I didn't have much time to communicate because I was talking with Mr. Steiner but it was my first advisor who was more informed of the technical details which we informed -- reported to SRSG. But during that conversation, as I said earlier, he was willing to go and fetch Mr. Limaj as Ljubijana airport and bring him to Kosova to meet his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, finally this: At the time of his arrest, were you aware that Fatmir Limaj communicated an address to the citizens of Kosovo about the circumstances in which he was being arrested and how they should regard this matter?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: Yes. When we contacted him, when we heard that the Prosecutor had made public the indictment in Podgorica and that he had got this information from a reporter of Reuters agency, and then later he had made to statement to this reporter in which Mr. Fatmir Limaj informed the citizens of Kosova of his arrest -- initially of his readiness to surrender voluntarily and then of the following arrest. And in addition to that statement, he appealed to the citizens of Kosova to be calm, to respect the ICTY, and that he was innocent, and that his innocence -- he will prove his innocence before the Court. And that it was in the interests of Kosova for the citizens to be responsible, maintain a calm stand, not cause violence or riots but respect all the actions of the ICTY because no individual is more worthy than the future of Kosova. These were more or less the words Mr. Fatmir Limaj used in that statement. That was an important statement which affected -- which accounted for lack of demonstrations, use of violence, and instability in Kosova. Myself as former prime minister and the citizens at large were not prepared for such an act; therefore, Mr. Fatmir Limaj's appeal, which I heard afterward broadcast by Kosova radio television, played a positive impact on Kosova citizens being calm and accepting this painful event in a dignified matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: To round that off, I think it's right to say that the arrests on this occasion were the first arrests of any Albanians vis-a-vis the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM REXHEPI
utterances.text: If you allow me, Your Honours, I'd like to inform you that we had received information about the arrests of three members of the KLA, the two accused and by mistake Agim Murtezi, but Fatmir Limaj's arrest was the first arrest as a senior politician. The arrest was still confusing. We didn't know why the three persons arrested were arrested until a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. In fact it may be appropriate -- I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have to questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you receiving a translation? There seems to be a confusion of translation channels at that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was indicating that there seems to be no question about your evidence so that we must thank you for your attendance and your assistance and indicate that you're now free to return to Kosovo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will adjourn now and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'm grateful. I'm asked for a moment just to address Your Honours about a particular subject matter which arose yesterday. And it concerns, I'm afraid, the rather thorny topic of disclosure. And I appreciate today that the Prosecution have filed a response to our motion concerning the disclosure of exculpatory material. However, this matter, in our submission, is somewhat more fundamental even than that. And I appreciate that you may be in the imminent future delivering a decision in relation to that motion and response. So this is really a footnote to that but raising a further dimension. If you could be handed - we've had copies made - a statement made by a member of the British armed services named Christopher Clark. There should be one for each of you in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You will see that that statement was taken over a number of days in 2001 and therefore has been in existence since then and plainly known to the Prosecution. You will see from the number of pages that it is in fact a detailed statement, and you will also see by merely looking at the first page that he's a deeply experienced member of the British armed services in terms of the various tasks that he's qualified to undertake and has undertaken over 16 years with the British Army. And you will see on that page that he was seconded to the KVM, Kosovo Verification Mission, in October 1998. The rest of the statement deals with his knowledge of and contacts with, to some extent the Serb regime - he mentions it on page 3 - but also with, in particular, the KLA to such an extent that members of his team were deputed to effectively live with the KLA in order to perform their task. So it's a statement which has intimate information and opinion as well about the KLA in 1998. Without going into -- into that detail, we would submit that this statement was plainly relevant from the beginning to these proceedings as a whole. We learnt about it for the first time yesterday afternoon. And it was immediately obvious to all of us that it was relevant. Perhaps I don't need to expound on why it's relevant, but there are two respects in which it is. One, to a very general broad point flagged in our pre-trial brief concerning armed conflict and the jurisdictional aspect of these proceedings. But it is also relevant to the potential liability, certainly of the defendant that I represent vis-a-vis the command structure said to exist within the KLA and therefore his responsibility within that, possibly, for offences alleged on this indictment. Therefore, on those two fronts alone, this statement should have been disclosed whether or not the Prosecution were intending to rely upon it. We're not entirely clear why it wasn't disclosed at an early stage when it was first seen because even if at the stage it was first seen it may not have been perceived to be relevant to a topic, for example, on armed conflict that may or may not arise because there were no pre-trial briefs served at that time. It must have been clear it was likely to be reasonably brought up during these proceedings, even not -- if not clearly delineated by then, at that earlier stage. But in any event, so far as the command structure itself and any liability arising under it, it must have been clear that that was something of considerable importance from the beginning. And in fact, the statement actually indicates that there are three key people in the KLA, and the three key people, in fact one of them is the next witness. The other two, one of whom you've heard this week, the other during the Prosecution case. So those three key people are indicated to be people without whom decisions and operations did not take place. So there can't have been any doubt from the beginning that this statement was relevant. Now, either the system of disclosure is substantially and seriously defective for this to have arisen at this very late stage -- and may I say, just as I may take a slight detour at this stage to indicate to Your Honours why I am raising it now. We are nearing the end of Mr. Limaj's case, and you may be gratified to learn that it will be this week. We have substantially reduced, with the knowledge of the Prosecution and notice to the Prosecution, the number of witnesses we were intending to call. There are now just two live witnesses remaining; one who is now here this afternoon and one who we've brought forward from next week but the earliest he can be here is Friday. He is, if I may put it, a character witness; he is very short. So it will not in any way impinge upon the schedule for Friday. So therefore, rather than wait until the end of our case, I raise it now that the system of disclosure here is seriously defective. And whilst one can understand on occasions that with the vast amount of material, things may be forgotten or overlooked or even deemed to be not relevant, none of those reservations can apply to this statement. And plainly, even if it had got overlooked prior to the beginning of the case when the pre-trial briefs had already been lodged, the system should have an ability to review - certainly in other jurisdictions called rolling review - to review material as the case develops. Plainly, that did not happen here because if it had it would have been disclosed before -- well before Christmas of last year, and of course would have been available to us at the time that I cross-examined Crosland and that Mr. Harvey cross-examined Coo; and, for that matter, of course for the briefing and eventual evidence of the Defence witness, Mr. Churcher, who will now have to be asked about this matter. And if he has further observations we may ask for permission for a supplemental statement from him. So it's come all in the wrong order. And I'm not standing here to make, I hope, a fair and reasonable criticism, but because we are concerned for the future. We do not wish a situation to arise in which in a week's time or two weeks' time, as gradually we get towards the final brief stage, we have more material. You will recall in fact just at the end of the Prosecution case we had the statement from Mr. Thaqi served upon us. Well, at that stage, it was being said, it had been overlooked; and that no doubt will be a matter within the motion already filed. However, it demonstrates, in my submission, that there's something - sometimes wrongly put - wrong in the state of Denmark, but I hesitate to use particular phrases from Shakespeare. But there is in fact something seriously wrong with that which is going on within this state, that is the state of the Prosecution. We would ask at this stage not only for the measures that are contained in our motion but that with immediate effect somebody within the Prosecution team immediately does a proper and thorough review of material again in case there is yet more of this substance to be revealed. And as I say, at the moment there is just time to deal with it; but in fact, in fairness to these defendants, this is material we should have had laid before us at the beginning. So I hope I have put it clearly, but that is what we are asking: an immediate review. And we are saying that this is not only unfortunate but unfair that it's come at this time. But as with all the other things in this case, we are prepared to, as it were, pick it up and run with it, and we will. But as you may imagine, we are deeply concerned about what else there may be within the portals of the Prosecution beyond that same door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The door again. Do I understand that you seek nothing specific concerning this statement or this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I should have added -- Your Honour is quite right. In fact, the Prosecution have been kind enough to indicate -- because we obviously want to call him if he can be found. They're prepared to allow this document to be admitted under 92 bis. So I will be asking for it to be tendered under that particular regulation. So that's the position so far -- this is material you will be seeing in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I support those submissions by Mr. Mansfield, make it clear in doing so beyond that which he's asked for in relation to Clark, I seek no ruling but to add to it in two respects. Firstly, to confirm that matters are moving on at a pace. I understand from my learned friends Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Harvey that they anticipate starting and concluding the case of Mr. Bala next week. It may well be that my case will start at the end of next week. And looking at the timetable that we are actively discussing between my team and my lay client, that is not a case that is going to last perhaps anything like the length that was predicted at the close of the Prosecution's case or even by us while Mr. Mansfield's case was and is ongoing. Therefore, these matters are urgent. We are drafting, and Mr. Whiting and his team will have from us tonight, a letter on behalf of our client requesting disclosure of all material in the possession of the OTP that is or might be deployed to be used in cross-examination of Defence witnesses called on behalf of Musliu. May I, as it were, support the theme of Mr. Mansfield's submission simply by a few lines from May on international criminal evidence at paragraph 5.25, at page 151. Forgive me, time has not permitted a photocopy. I was not aware Mr. Mansfield was going to make the submission he made until I literally walked into court. But it simply says this: "The Prosecution cannot hold back evidence that goes to the heart of the case as a matter of tactics in order to use it in cross-examination of the accused." And to that word I respectfully add and/or any witness called by the accused. "This was emphasised in Krstic where the Prosecution confronted General Krstic with an intercept of a conversation between himself and another Bosnian Serb during which the accused used a pejorative term to describe Bosnian Muslims and was alleged to say 'kill them all.' The Trial Chamber found Prosecution made a tactical decision to use this intercept during cross-examination rather than during its case in chief to 'explosive' effect, and since it went to a fundamental part of the Prosecution's case, namely specific intent of a genocide case, it was not admissible in rebuttal." I simply pause to reflect upon that part of the cross-examination of Mr. Selimi there was also about matters explosive and whether it could be properly said that prior notice at least of the possession of that material in the hands of Prosecutor was appropriate to be disclosed; I understand it was not. So, Your Honour, in those respects, in that regard and for these reasons, I support and slightly develop my learned friend's submissions just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. -- oh, Mr. Guy-Smith, were you holding your fire until this time, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have -- I join in the remarks made by my colleagues. I'm somewhat troubled at the stage that we're in at this time. I trust - and I use the word as a hope - that that information that may exist at this time within the Prosecution's possession, that they intend on using with regard to cross-examination of any of the witnesses that we will be tendering on behalf of Mr. Bala, we are made aware of in the manner that Mr. Topolski has just raised. I also do request the remedy because I think it's a remedy that we seek as opposed to a comment of what's going on. I do request the remedy that at this point someone at the office goes through the information that they have and makes very, very, very sure that we've got all that we should have. And that the -- and that the -- the notion here is not one of I think penury, but rather duty with regard to the kinds of information that should be furnished an accused in any proceedings and certainly in proceedings such as these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to this statement I don't completely share Mr. Mansfield's characterisation of the relevance of this statement; however, having said that, I do not dispute in any way that it should have -- that it should have been disclosed. It was not disclosed. And on behalf of the Prosecutor, I take responsibility for that. It was -- it was overlooked and I would submit that this -- this -- even in an -- in conjunction with the various other matters that were raised in the motion that was filed by the Defence last week and that we have responded to today, do not warrant the kind of remedy that is being sought by the Defence. In this particular instance, we have agreed to what I think is an adequate remedy, and that is to put this statement in 92 bis. If the -- and in fact we have already started to try to locate this person so that the 92 bis procedure can be done. If there were other remedies sought such as recall of witnesses or further submissions that were alluded to, I'm sure that's also something that can be done and the Prosecution would be quite open to, depending on the details. The -- I'm not going to go through our detailed response that we filed today; however, I'll just anticipate that the -- it's the Prosecution's position that the Prosecution has put into place with the knowledge of the Defence a very detailed and thorough process of review which has captured thousands of pages of materials which have been disclosed to the Defence. There have been a few instances - and I underline a few instances - where the process has not worked; that happens. With a case of this magnitude, with the volume of documents in the possession of the Prosecution, with the developments of issues as they've gone through the trial, those things happen. It's regrettable; it happens. They -- I would submit that every time it's happened it's been remedied and -- including this very last time. However, those few instances where this has occurred -- and I would submit in -- it's actually quite a remarkable record given the circumstances. Those few instances simply do not warrant the kind of enormous, broad remedy that is being sought by the Defence, which would, frankly speaking, require the trial to stop for quite a period if the Prosecution were to undertake to re-review all of the material in its possession. But those matters are more completely addressed in the Prosecution's response. With respect to the second issue which was raised by Mr. Topolski and joined by Mr. Bala, I have not received the letter, I have not fully thought out the Prosecution's position on the request; however, I do know that the case that Mr. Topolski cited to, the Krstic case. What is the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. known as the "kill them all" tape is not applicable in this case. It's not the -- the issue in that case was whether, as Mr. Topolski mentioned as he discussed it, the issue was -- as I understand it, I could be wrong, but as I understand it in that case is whether the tape could then come into evidence; it's not whether it could be used on cross-examination. The other -- the other thing was that that tape - and I think this is discussed in the opinion - is a -- it's obviously that it was of a wholly -- it was a tape of the accused himself and it was a wholly different category to anything that we are talking about here about documents or other things concerning Defence witnesses. I think the Court on this issue was quite clear about what the Rules are, and in fact today I disclosed to Mr. Mansfield two documents that I may use in the cross-examination of this next witness, who has yet to testify. One of those was -- had already been disclosed to the Defence under the ordinary disclosure procedures. I disclosed a translation. And the other document is not directly relevant to this case; it's concerns a different time period, but it may arise in cross-examination. I disclosed that as well. So those are -- that's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you sit, Mr. Whiting, a little more, please, on how this document came to light. I take it you accept that it's been in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor since 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It came to light most recently actually in a review that I was doing - it came to my attention because it was caught in a -- in a -- in an ISU search, ISU standing for information support unit. This is more completely explained in our response - for this next witness and it came up that way because this next witness is mentioned in the document. It should have been captured earlier. There are other names in there where it should have been captured. I can't say why it wasn't. That's how it most recently came to my attention. I have seen this statement before but read it a long time ago, either before this case was even indicted or at the very beginning and have simply forgotten about it. But when this issue -- when the issue in -- that's addressed in the statement became -- became an issue in this case, which I would submit was when the Defence filed their pre-trial brief, at that time, this -- this statement certainly was never in my mind. I never thought about it. And it only came to my attention the other day -- I believe it was yesterday or the day before yesterday. And I immediately, upon seeing the statement, disclosed it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I understand from that that you have in fact been running or have completed running searches directed to the names of all people who are not only your witnesses but the potential witnesses for the Defence in this case through the system that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When we got the names of the potential Defence witnesses, we -- as the Court is aware, there were approximately 60 names. It's impractical to have ISU searches run for all 60 names. So we had to make a decision on doing it in stages, which we have been doing, trying to anticipate -- when we come to know that witnesses, Defence witnesses were going to come to be called, we would run -- we would run the names. It takes some time for the search to be run and then the review of the search, given the pace and the timing of the -- these events, a review of the searches has tended to occur only days before -- and in some cases the morning of a witness testifying. So to more directly -- to more -- to absolutely clearly answer the Court's question, we have run searches on some but not all of the Defence witnesses. We have reviewed the searches on some but not all of the Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So there is a possibility that even in that review of the Prosecution's material, there might be revealed some additional document or documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It shouldn't be the case, but anything is possible because of course these documents should be caught by other reviews, other searches that have been done or reviews that have been done. The process is an overlapping searching process. So documents come up again and again in reviews, though that doesn't always happen and it can happen that a document is overlooked. So it's not likely that that will happening; it is possible that that will happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it you are searching under names. Are you searching on any other basis, any subject basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Again, this is laid out in some more detail in our response that we filed today, but we searched under names and we searched also under certain places that were particularly pertinent. For example, Lapusnik; that was searched a long time ago and that was reviewed. It should be said that the -- a list of all the search criteria, all the searches we were going to do, that list was provided very early on to the Defence maybe in -- in July of 2003. And the Defence were invited to provide any additional search names that they thought would be appropriate; none were provided. As a practical matter, the name searches are -- tend to be of witnesses or, obviously, the accused. Those tend to be the searches that are done for this kind of a review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So do you have a facility to search by subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, for example, if you searched by -- for example, if you search by "General Staff," the problem is you would get approximately 2 million documents because there's -- "General Staff" appears so many different contexts. So the problem with subject matter is defining it narrowly enough so that you come up with a meaningful number of documents to be able to review. Certainly, I haven't fully thought it through, but certainly if there are particular subject matters which can be searched in a helpful way, that's certainly something that could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, it appears that there will be a significant reduction in the number of Defence witnesses to be called. If you were provided the names of those who are to be called, would it be feasible in the next few days for those to be run again and for them to be -- the resulting information to be reviewed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the answer is yes, though the devil's in the details. For example, if we got the -- today's Wednesday. If we got the list today, we could submit it immediately -- I assume we could -- we would have it back tomorrow morning? Mr. Black is the -- our local expert on these issues. It takes a day or two to complete the searches and for them to come back. The material that comes back can range from a little packet that's less than an inch thick to several binders of materials. Those -- those can be reviewed with relative speed. Now, of course we have already with respect to the Musliu witnesses, we've already one some of those searches because of course some of the -- when we received the names of the alibi witnesses we ran those searches already. So it's possible that we have done some or even all of them. So that's why I say the devil's in the details. It's certainly feasible; it may take more or less time depending on when we get it and how many witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On a different topic, Mr. Whiting, you did indicate that you had provided to Mr. Mansfield today documents that you would be putting to his next witness, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That I may put to the next witness, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a course of conduct that you will now be following for all witnesses of all accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we were going to be guided by the Prosecution -- by the Court's guidance on this issue that was provided -- I can't remember when if it was yesterday or the day before, that that is if it's been -- if it's already been disclosed, then there's not a burden on the Prosecution to flag-up the document. The reason I provided these documents today is, number one, the -- with respect to the first document which had already been disclosed, it was just a translation and I thought in fairness they should have a -- the translation that we had. That's been our practice; whenever we translate any document, we provide that. And secondly, the other document, to my knowledge, had not been disclosed. Frankly speaking, I didn't even check because I can't imagine that it was disclosed. I can't see any reason why it would have been disclosed. So that to me seemed it was proper to then disclose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, without going into your response which we have just received, I've skimmed through it and listened to both sides. What's not clear to me, at least - it may be clear to others - is the difference between the ISU and what is available generally, not only to counsel but to everyone, through the other electronic system you described with the acronym EDS, which stands for electronic disclosure system. I take it that you're not meaning the fact that counsel could avail themselves of that opportunity would have made the Prosecution discharge its disclosure obligation? That's the first question. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Fine. Let's go to the other one then. What's the difference as far as scope between the ISU and the EDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The difference is that the ISU searches all collections within the possession of the Prosecution. The EDS is a subset of that group. The EDS contains -- the EDS has two -- to get into the details of this, the EDS has two different parts to it; the first is is the general collection, the second is the case-specific collection. The general collection contains I think literally millions of pages of documents which tend to be documents that are disclosed -- where there's no security concern, there's no restriction, they can be disclosed to anybody. They're searchable by all Defence counsel on all teams and they're searchable by name. The case-specific part of the EDS is only accessible by the Defence counsel in this case, and that contains documents which are -- which only pertain to this case. It -- those are -- what's contained in there is what we have disclosed otherwise. So the case-specific disclosures occur, are given in hard copy, on CD, and then are put in the EDS so that they can be searched in the EDS. To -- those two parts of the EDS together, however, form a subset - a large subset, but nonetheless a subset - of what is searched by the ISU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything further, Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, if I may. I think what has been said this afternoon raises a really rather serious issue, not just for this particular case in this particular part of the Tribunal but for all cases being heard in the Tribunal at the moment. Now, as the song goes, I may be old-fashioned, however the system of disclosure that's been described electronically is plainly a failure. What was interesting was the - and I'm going to call it an old-fashioned word, perhaps not a computer-friendly word - what are the triggers that have to be pulled in order to get the information that's necessary? The idea that this recent statement is only triggered at this late stage by a search for names is a nonsense; of course there are names in here and if triggering names means anything, then this statement should have been triggered about -- well, I don't want to overestimate it, but given the number of names in here that are relevant to this case, on many occasions before now, one being obviously Jakup Krasniqi, who gave evidence many weeks ago now. But of course, we say in a sensible system of disclosure in the old days where one had bits of paper and card, you'd have topics. So, for example -- I don't know whether there are these topics within this electronic system. So another way of approaching this is not by looking for names, but it might be by looking for the word "KLA." It might be by looking for the word "zone." It might be by looking for the word "Pastrik." It might be by looking for the word "weapons." All of which have been discussed. They're details. The most obviously word is "armed conflict." If it's not been filed under "armed conflict," the question is why hasn't it been filed under "armed conflict" in the first place? I don't want to go too far down this road, but I think Your Honours will see where I'm going here. It is of course a humanly-driven system; it depends on the quality of the people operating it. It depends on the quality of the information that's being put into it in the first place and how it's being logged so it can go retrieved.
